title: CDNs & Edge Caching
summary: How a CDN gets content physically close to users and the caching rules — and pitfalls — that keep it correct.

slides.markdown:
A **CDN (Content Delivery Network)** is a set of servers geographically spread out — **edge locations** or **points of presence (PoPs)** — that cache your content close to users, instead of every request crossing the globe to one origin server.

- Distance is latency: physics puts a floor on how fast a round trip to a far-away server can be.
- The CDN answers most requests from a nearby edge cache; only cache misses go back to origin.
- Getting caching *correct* — knowing what's safe to cache and for how long — is the hard part, not the distribution.

slides.subTitle: Distance is latency
slides.markdown:
Light in fiber travels at roughly two-thirds the speed of light in vacuum — a round trip from Mumbai to a server in Virginia is bound by that speed limit no matter how fast the server itself is. At ~13,000km, that's already 60-90ms of unavoidable propagation delay each way, before the server does any work.

A CDN's fix isn't making the network faster — it's making the trip **shorter**: replicate content at edge locations near users, so a user in Mumbai hits a PoP in Mumbai (single-digit ms) instead of Virginia. Compute-bound work still has to reach the origin; static/cacheable content doesn't.

![One origin server far from users vs a CDN's edge PoPs serving from nearby locations](assets/cdn-origin-vs-edge.svg)

Every edge PoP holds a cached copy of content it's served before; the origin only sees traffic for content no nearby edge has cached yet, or content explicitly marked as never-cacheable.

assets.alt: One origin server far from users vs a CDN's edge PoPs serving from nearby locations

slides.markdown:
How does a request find the *nearest* edge? Two common mechanisms:

- **DNS-based routing** — the CDN's DNS server answers differently depending on where the query came from, returning the IP of a close PoP.
- **Anycast** — the same IP is announced from many PoPs via BGP; normal routing (shortest AS-path) sends a client's packets to whichever PoP is topologically closest. See [interdomain-routing-bgp](interdomain-routing-bgp).

Anycast works at the IP layer with no DNS dependency; DNS-based routing is more flexible for load-aware steering.

Every request an edge PoP receives is either a **hit** (the PoP already has a valid cached copy — serves it instantly, origin never involved) or a **miss** (nothing cached, or it expired). On a miss, the edge does an **origin pull**: it fetches the content from origin, serves it to the user, *and* caches it — so the next nearby request for the same thing is a hit.

The first request for any given piece of content anywhere is always a miss (or close to it) — CDNs get their speedup from repeat traffic, not the very first fetch.

How long a CDN caches something is decided by response headers, not guessed:

- **`Cache-Control: max-age=3600`** — cacheable for an hour, then revalidate or re-fetch.
- **`Cache-Control: no-store`** — never cache, full stop (e.g. a payment confirmation).
- **`ETag`** — a content fingerprint; on expiry, the CDN can ask origin "has this changed?" and get a cheap `304 Not Modified` instead of re-downloading.

Getting these headers right *is* the caching strategy. See [http-fundamentals](http-fundamentals).

slides.subTitle: Cache invalidation is hard
slides.markdown:
**Cache invalidation** — telling every edge PoP holding a stale copy to drop it *now* — is famously one of the two hard problems in computer science. You update an image; it's cached at 200 PoPs with 24 hours left on its TTL, and some users keep seeing the old version until either the TTL expires or you issue an explicit **purge**.

Purges aren't instant globally, and purging too broadly is expensive and slow. The pragmatic answer many teams use: version filenames (`app.v2.js`) so "updating" means serving a *new* URL, sidestepping invalidation entirely.

Not all content caches the same way:

- **Static content** (images, JS/CSS, video) — identical for every user, safe to cache long, versioned filenames make invalidation trivial.
- **Dynamic content** (a personalized feed, a per-user API response) — often uncacheable at a shared edge, or cacheable only briefly and per-user.

Modern CDNs blur this with **edge compute** — but the baseline holds: cache what's identical for everyone, don't cache what isn't.

| | CDN edge caching | App-level cache (Redis) |
|---|---|---|
| Lives | Near users, geographically distributed | Near your application/database |
| Caches | HTTP responses, static assets | Query results, computed objects, sessions |
| Granularity | Whole responses, by URL | Arbitrary keys your app defines |
| Typical win | Network latency, origin load | Database/compute load |

They solve different bottlenecks and commonly coexist. See [caching fundamentals](caching-fundamentals) for the app-level side.

slides.subTitle: Hit vs miss
slides.markdown:
![Request path showing a cache hit served instantly from edge vs a miss falling through to origin](assets/cdn-hit-vs-miss-path.svg)

The hit path never leaves the edge; the miss path adds a full round trip to origin — which is exactly why cache **hit rate** is the metric CDN operators watch most closely, not raw traffic volume.

assets.alt: Request path showing a cache hit served instantly from edge vs a miss falling through to origin

slides.subTitle: Caching a personalized response
slides.markdown:
A dangerous mistake: **caching a personalized or authenticated response at a shared edge node.** If `/account/dashboard` returns *User A's* data and gets cached with a generic key (just the URL, ignoring the auth cookie), the next user hitting that same edge PoP for `/account/dashboard` can be served **User A's cached response** — a real data leak, not a theoretical one.

The fix: never cache responses that vary by identity unless the cache key includes the identity (or, simpler, mark them `no-store`/`private`). This is one of the most common CDN misconfiguration incidents in practice.
